title.text:
Prompting and
reasoning models

objects.text: How do I get reliable work out of an assistant?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 8 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome to Session 8. Last time we opened the model file and saw why size and licence decide rent, host or own. Today is about what you type. A prompt is a brief to a new colleague, and like any brief it can be weak or strong. I will show recorded runs of both, a structured answer a program can check, and a calculation that one prompt got wrong and another got right.

slides.notes:
Here is what you leave with today. You can write a prompt as a brief with five parts and test it on a checked set. You can ask for a table or JSON so the answer can be checked. And you can say what the vendors advise for reasoning models, and check a calculation yourself.

The checking matters as much as the writing, because a confident answer can still be wrong.

title.text:
Your two hours: briefs, recorded
runs, then your own prompt

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_4ad48d6c.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: You rewrite a weak prompt on paper with the five-part checklist.

slides.notes:
Today has three big parts. First thirty-five minutes on the ideas: a prompt as a brief with five parts, examples, a fixed output format, testing a prompt on a checked set, and what vendors say about reasoning models. Then twenty-five minutes of recorded runs, including one where a plain prompt got a payroll sum wrong.

After the break you rewrite a weak prompt on paper, using the five-part checklist, and decide which of your own prompts to test first.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is the difference between open source and open weights?
2.  How big is the weights file of a model with 7 billion numbers at 2 bytes each?
3.  Is GGUF a container or a level of compression?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 7. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is the difference between open source and open weights? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Open weights means the trained numbers can be downloaded, under a licence that may still limit use. Open Source AI in the OSI sense also needs the training code, information about the training data and a licence without use limits.

Question two. How big is the weights file of a model with 7 billion numbers at 2 bytes each? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. About 14 GB. Parameters times bytes per number, with working memory needed on top.

Question three. Is GGUF a container or a level of compression? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. A container. The number of bits per number is a separate choice called quantisation, and a GGUF file can hold 16-bit or 4-bit numbers.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

A model that works through a problem before it replies. Some assistants let you switch this on.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Prompt. Anything you type to an assistant.

Brief. A prompt written once, in parts, and reused. Like a task handed to a new colleague.

Example prompt. A finished example inside the prompt that shows the format you want. Also called a few-shot prompt.

Structured output. An answer in a fixed shape, such as a table or JSON, so that it can be checked.

Reasoning model. A model that works through a problem before it replies. Some assistants let you switch this on.

title.text:
A good prompt is a brief to a colleague
who knows nothing about your company

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_brief_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A good prompt is a brief to a colleague who knows nothing about your company

objects.text: Give the role, the context, examples, the format and the checks.

runs.text: A prompt is anything you type.
A brief is a prompt written once, in parts, and reused.

slides.notes:
Imagine a new accountant on day one. You would not say, write the report. You would say who they are writing for, what format you want, what to leave out, and what to do if a figure is missing. A prompt works the same way. The assistant knows nothing about your company or your reader.

Five parts cover most briefs: the role, the context, examples, the format, and the checks. Here they are on the Monday sales email from our case company. The words prompt and brief are different. Anything you type is a prompt. A brief is the one you write once, check, and reuse.

title.text:
Demonstration 1: the same data
with a weak and a strong brief

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_briefs_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 1: the same data with a weak and a strong brief

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Recorded runs, Claude fresh subagent sessions, 4 November 2026. Not ChatGPT or Gemini.
Both runs got the figures right.
Only the strong brief followed a format, and it said what the data cannot explain.

slides.notes:
Both prompts gave the assistant the same sales data. The weak one said only, write the Monday sales email. The strong one named the role and the reader, set the format, said to use only these figures, and said to admit what the data cannot explain. These are recorded runs from 4 November.

In both, the figures came out right. The weak run chose its own layout, added advice to keep beans and sugar in stock because demand is rising, which nobody asked for, and left a placeholder for my name. The strong run followed the format and ended with one thing to check. Same data, different brief.

title.text:
Five parts make a brief: role, context,
format, checks and an example

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_fivepart_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Five parts make a brief: role, context, format, checks and an example

objects.text: The strong brief from the recorded run. It had no example. Add one when the format matters.

slides.notes:
Here is the strong brief taken apart. The role: you are the sales analyst. The context: who reads it. The format: a subject line, a two-sentence summary, a table, at most three plain sentences. The checks: use only these figures, do not invent a number, cause or customer, and say so if something cannot be explained.

The fifth part is missing in this brief. There is no example. When the format really matters, paste one finished email and say, write the next one like this. Anthropic and Google list examples among their advice. OpenAI says to try its reasoning models with none first. All three stress clear instructions and a stated format.

title.text:
An example shows the format
faster than a description does

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_fewshot_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: An example shows the format faster than a description does

objects.text: Show two finished cases, then give the new one.

runs.text: Google advises varied examples that all use the same layout.
Google warns that too many examples can make a model overfit to them.

slides.notes:
Think of a new clerk and a stack of forms. Instead of describing the filing rules for ten minutes, you show two forms already filled in and say, do the next one like these. That is an example prompt, also called few-shot. Here two messages carry their labels and the third is the new case.

The examples fix the labels and the layout. Google’s guide advises varied examples with identical formatting, Google’s prompting guide also warns that too many examples can make the model overfit to them. I describe that as a danger of copying the examples too closely, so test on cases that differ from them. One or two good examples are usually enough to try first.

title.text: Mark the data off from the instructions

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_delims_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Mark the data off from the instructions

objects.text: Put the data between clear markers, like a folder behind a cover sheet.

runs.text: OpenAI’s guide for reasoning models suggests delimiters such as markdown or XML tags.
A marker does not make text safe. Sessions 10 and 11 show why.

slides.notes:
In an office, a cover sheet says what to do and a folder holds the papers. The clerk knows which is which. In a prompt you build the same structure with markers. The instructions come first. Then a line such as three hash signs, messages start, then the data, then messages end.

OpenAI’s guide for its reasoning models suggests delimiters like markdown or XML tags to separate the parts. The markers help the model see where the data is. They do not make the data safe. A message can contain an order, and the assistant may follow it. We return to that in Sessions 10 and 11.

title.text:
Demonstration 2: ask for JSON,
and a program can check the reply

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_structured_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 2: ask for JSON, and a program can check the reply

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Recorded run, Claude fresh subagent, 6 November 2026. One run.
Four messages came back as four records with fixed fields.
The highlighted fields are the type and the urgency.

slides.notes:
Now structured output. JSON is a plain-text format with named fields, which any program can read. I gave the assistant four invented customer messages from Nile Valley Foods and a list of exact fields: customer, type, items, amount, urgency, reference. The prompt said, use only what the message says and use null if a field is missing.

This is message three, the leaking jerrycans. The record names the type as complaint, the six unusable jerrycans, and the urgency as high. A table works the same way for a person reading. The point is that a fixed format can be checked.

title.text:
A fixed format let a program check the
shape and a person find two loose fields

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_checkgrid_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A fixed format let a program check the shape and a person find two loose fields

objects.text: Fix to try: split the reference into invoice number and payment reference, then run again.

slides.notes:
I checked the reply in two ways. A short program confirmed that it was valid JSON, with four records and exactly the fields I asked for. Then I read each field against the message. Everything matched except two. For message one, the customer came back as Mary and the shop name in one field.

For message two, the invoice number and the mobile money reference came back joined in one field, because my prompt allowed only one reference. The fault lies in my brief, and the answer was fine. The cure is to split the field and run it again. Format checks catch the shape. A person still checks the meaning.

title.text:
Prompts are tested on a
checked set, like anything else

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_promptlog_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Prompts are tested on a checked set, like anything else

objects.text: Keep a prompt log: version, change, runs, result. Small sets show a pattern and prove nothing.

slides.notes:
A prompt is something you test, as you test a new supplier. Write it, run it on a set of cases where you already know the right answer, score the answers, change one thing, and run it again. Anthropic’s guide says to define success criteria and some way to test against them before you start refining.

Keep a log. Mine shows the payroll prompt in two versions, with two runs each, and the orders prompt with one run. Later I split the payroll prompt into four versions, to test one change at a time. Look at the Right column. Two runs is a small set.

A real set has ten or more cases. Which task of yours has cases with known answers?

title.text:
Demonstration 3: one calculation, four
prompts, changing one thing at a time

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_payroll_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 3: one calculation, four prompts, changing one thing at a time

objects.text: Ten recorded runs, 9 right. Plain 1 of 2; plain + re-add 3 of 3; framed 3 of 3; framed + re-add 2 of 2.

slides.notes:
A payroll case with several steps: overtime at two rates, an unpaid leave day, pension on gross pay, and an advance repaid after pension. I worked out the key separately and checked it twice. My first comparison was unfair: the framed prompt differed from the plain one in two ways, the framing and a closing sentence to re-add the lines.

So I made two controlled variants, each changing one thing. Plain: 1 of 2 right. Plain plus the re-add sentence: 3 of 3. Framed without the re-add sentence: 3 of 3. Framed with it: 2 of 2. Only the plain run, with neither, was wrong. Each change may help, but ten runs cannot say which, or how much. A pattern in a small set, not proof.

title.text:
The wrong plain run was 200,000 out,
showed every line and sounded sure

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_slip_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The wrong plain run was 200,000 out, showed every line and sounded sure

objects.text: Re-add it yourself: 1,800,000 plus 337,500 minus 81,818.

runs.text: The key gives 2,055,682.
Plain run 2 wrote 1,855,682.
Re-add the lines that matter.

slides.notes:
This is the wrong run, line by line. Every step was shown and the tone was calm. But the gross pay added up to 1,855,682, and the key says 2,055,682. A slip of 200,000 shillings, and every figure after it was wrong, the net pay and the total cost.

You can catch this in a minute with a calculator: salary, plus overtime, minus the leave deduction. That is the habit. Ask for the working so that you can check it, and recompute the figure that everything else depends on. Neither a calm tone nor the shown working proves a sum is right.

title.text:
A reasoning model works through
the problem before it answers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_reasoning_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A reasoning model works through the problem before it answers

objects.text: Vendors describe this differently. Their own words are on the slide after this.

slides.notes:
In Session 6 you met reasoning models. Here is the practical picture. A standard model answers straight away. A reasoning model, or a standard assistant with its thinking switched on, spends extra time working through the problem before it replies. That can help with multi-step problems like the payroll sum.

It also takes longer, and the thinking can add to the bill, so it is not the right choice for every task. I did not record a reasoning model against a standard one today. A fresh session has no thinking switch, so I will show that live on the assistant you use.

title.text:
The vendor guides agree: state
the goal and the limits, then test

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_vendors_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The vendor guides agree: state the goal and the limits, then test

objects.text: Guides read on 6 November 2026. Product names and settings change often.

slides.notes:
Here is what each vendor says, in its own terms, and I add nothing. OpenAI’s guide for its reasoning models says to use short, direct prompts, and that asking for step-by-step reasoning is unnecessary and can sometimes hurt. Anthropic says its models can think before answering, and that newer models decide how much, with an effort setting.

Google says its Gemini thinking models reason on their own, so you usually need not ask for steps. On testing they agree in spirit: a precise end goal, success criteria, and iterate. So for a reasoning model, state the problem, the rules and the output, and leave the working to it.

title.text:
Demonstration 4, live: the same
prompt with thinking off, then on

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_b02120ae.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 4, live: the same prompt with thinking off, then on

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Live, on your assistant. Results vary from run to run.
Time taken and the length of the answer.
Whether the net pay matches the key.

slides.notes:
Now a live demonstration, on the assistant you use, and nothing here is recorded. Many assistants have a switch that lets the model think longer. I paste the same framed payroll prompt twice, once with thinking off and once with it on. I note how long each takes and how long the answer is, and then I compare the net pay with the key, 1,802,898.

Results vary from run to run, so one try proves nothing. If your assistant has no such switch, we use the recorded runs instead. Whatever the result, the final step is the same: you check the figure that matters.

title.text:
Which kind of model to start
with depends on the task

rows.text: Well defined and quick; OpenAI says fast, defined tasks suit standard models
Extra working time can help; you still re-add the lines
Anything with money, law or people
Our plain run was wrong with every line shown

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_mail_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.50.png

objects.text: A starting view. Test it on your own cases, and ask your IT lead what the thinking costs.

slides.notes:
This is a starting view, and you test it. For well-defined jobs such as sorting messages, rewriting or a short summary, start with a standard model. OpenAI’s guide says fast, well-defined work suits its standard models, and that planning and ambiguous complex problems suit its reasoning models. For multi-step sums, plans or tangled rules, turn thinking on, and still re-add the lines.

And for anything involving money, law or people, either kind, followed by a check by hand. Our own plain run was wrong with every line shown. Ask your IT lead what thinking costs on the plan you use.

title.text:
Improve a weak prompt
with the five-part checklist

objects.text: 25 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Rewrite the weak prompt: "Reply to this customer complaint."

runs.text: Name the role and the reader.
Add the context: what happened, which customer.
Add one example, or write "none yet".
State the format and length.
Add the checks, and what to say when unsure.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_00c06284.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A rewritten prompt, checked against all five parts, ready for your log.

slides.notes:
This part is on paper, with no computer. Take the weak prompt on the slide, reply to this customer complaint, and rewrite it using the five parts. Name the role and the reader. Add the context: what happened and which customer. Add one example, or write none yet.

State the format and the length. Add the checks and what to say if the assistant is unsure. Then read your prompt aloud as if you were the new colleague. What would you still have to guess?

If your own task is better, use that. I will come round and read your drafts.

title.text:
Which of your prompts will
you test first, and how?

objects.text: Which prompt do you use often enough to test properly?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_pin_0.80.png

objects.text: Save it
Write it as a brief in the template.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.80.png

objects.text: Test it
Run it on ten cases with known answers.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_chart_0.80.png

objects.text: Structure it
Ask for a table or JSON so it can be checked.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.80.png

objects.text: Keep a person
Name who checks the figures before use.
Write the prompt, the first test and who checks it.

slides.notes:
Now your decision. Think of the prompt you use most often. Will you save it as a brief in the template?

Will you test it on ten cases where you know the right answer?

Will you ask for a table or JSON so that the answer can be checked?

Or will you name the person who checks the figures before anything is used?

Most prompts need two or three of these. Write down the prompt, the first test you will run, and who does the check. Which prompt did you choose, and what could it get wrong?

title.text:
Your five-part checklist grows into
the seven-part template you keep

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_template_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Your five-part checklist grows into the seven-part template you keep

objects.text: Templates/Reusable Brief Template.docx. Examples go with the inputs.

slides.notes:
You already have a template for this. The Reusable Brief Template has seven parts. The five-part checklist from today fits inside it. The goal and context cover the role and the reader. The output format is the format. How I will check is the checks. It adds three things, shown in red.

Inputs say exactly what you give the assistant, and that is also where an example goes. Constraints set length, tone and what to leave out. And what to say when unsure is the cheapest guard against an invented answer. Use the template, and record each version in your prompt log.

title.text:
Keep the template and the log,
and test every prompt you reuse

objects.text: What you keep from today

runs.text: A reusable prompt template and a prompt log, so that every prompt you keep has been tested.

objects.text: Our question today
How do I get reliable work out of an assistant?
Next session
Session 9: Giving a model your knowledge: retrieval, long context and fine-tuning. Bring one question that needs your own documents.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_4.10x4.50_227b1712.png

slides.notes:
Take the template and the prompt log. The template is the Reusable Brief Template you already have, and the log records each version, what changed and how many runs were right. Test every prompt before you reuse it. Next session is about giving a model your own knowledge: retrieval, long context and fine-tuning. Bring one question that needs your own documents.

We began with this question: How do I get reliable work out of an assistant? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
